newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia sees danger of world wheat war.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia sees danger of world wheat war.

text.p: Australia's A$4 billion wheat industry has swung from euphoria to a sense of dread as farmers begin to harvest a near-record crop amid a price slump so severe that it threatens a global wheat war led by Argentina, the European Union (EU) and the United States.
"Yes, we believe it (the prospect of a wheat war) is serious," Neil Fisher, executive director of Grains Council of Australia (GCA) told Reuters.

Australia's view of the ingredients of a back-to-1991/92 international grains war: worldwide surpluses from the present wheat crop; the surplus increased with Australia's own 21 million tonne crop; desperation in Argentina to unload wheat as fast as it can be harvested; EU subsidies on sales; and, most threateningly, the end of the U.S. presidential campaign.
"It's moving by the week," Fisher said.
Fisher's comments were sparked by the Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) cut in estimated pool wheat export prices by A$15.00 a tonne on Monday night, a move which GCA quickly branded as "disastrous".
But world wheat conflict has been obvious for months.
In Australia's view, Argentina set the fuse for a price war by unloading grain to solve infrastructure problems and to allow the sowing of summer crops.
"The Argentinians are having a pre-Christmas fire sale. They're very, very aggressive in the marketplace," Fischer said.
The EU, after increasing its wheat sale subsidies to A$20.00 a tonne from A$10.00 a tonne, responded to Argentina last week through a sale subsidised at A$30.00, Fischer said.
EU sales targets requiring it to move 250,000 tonnes of wheat a month would be increasingly difficult to meet without significant subsidies, he said.

The key to whether there is a full scale grains war, in the view of GCA and Australian brokers, is whether the U.S. breaks its eight-month retreat from use of its Export Enhancement Program (EEP) to weigh into a subsidy war with the EU.
"It really depends on the next month or two," Fisher said. USDA Secretary Richard Rominger early this year assured Australia that U.S. subsidies were not intended to damage Australian rural exports.

Australian grains industry leaders doubt this would mean much if U.S. feels drawn to retaliate against escalating EU subsidies. "What we're really fearful of is that once they've got the presidential election out of the way the (U.S. administration) will sit down and (decide not to) let the Europeans get away with this," Fisher said.
"(Then) we could be caught in the crossfire," Fisher said.
A still-tight world stocks-to-use ratio suggests there is no need for the U.S. to retaliate. "But logic doesn't always come into this equation and that's what really concerns us."
Futures broker Brendon Hillary of ANZ McCaughan Futures Ltd is one of those convinced by the logic of tight stocks. He does not see a strong imminent prospect of wheat war.
But, still, he believes prices will ultimately decide.
If Chicago wheat futures fall below $3.60 a bushel to about $3.40, EEP could come into play, Hillary said.
Hillary sees a floor price of about A$137.00 a tonne in Australian wheat futures with the relationship between pool, cash and futures prices. This view does not console Fisher.
The 1991/92 world wheat war, fuelled by subsidies of US$60.00/$70.00, dragged Australian pool prices to A$128.00 a tonne, he points out. "We got blown out of the water."
Australian Primary Industries Minister John Anderson will press the EU later this month on the issue.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
